title: Dropbox
prompt: Design a file storage and synchronization service like Dropbox. Users upload files from one device and have them available — and kept in sync — on every other device they're signed in on. Target ~500M users with an average of 2GB stored per user.

stages.title: Functional Requirements
stages.questionPrompt: What are the core functional requirements?
stages.howToAnswer: Focus on the must-have user actions. Sync, upload, download, sharing. Skip versioning and admin features unless asked.

must: Users can upload a file from any device
Files appear on other signed-in devices automatically
should: Conflict resolution when two devices edit at once
avoid: Drifting into Dropbox Paper / Spaces / collaboration features

stages.sampleAnswer:
1. Users can upload a file from any device.
2. The file appears on every other device the user is signed in on (sync).
3. Users can download any of their files.
4. Users can share a file with other users via a link or by adding their email.
hints: What is the user actually doing on each device? Upload, sync, download — and any social action like sharing.
Sync is the headline. Frame it as a user expectation, not an implementation: 'a file shows up where?'
Skip the desktop client UI and Dropbox Paper / Spaces — they're separate products.

stages.title: Non-Functional Requirements
stages.howToAnswer: Storage scale, durability, sync latency, bandwidth efficiency for large files. Quantify.

must: Durability — files must not be lost
Concrete sync latency target (seconds, not minutes)
avoid: Forgetting durability — this is the headline NFR
Conflating sync latency with upload latency

stages.sampleAnswer:
- Durability: 11 nines (no data loss).
- Sync latency: <5s p99 from upload completion to availability on a peer device.
- Scale: 500M users, 2GB avg → ~1 EB total. Read:write ~5:1.
- Bandwidth: never re-upload unchanged content (block-level dedupe).
- Availability: 99.9%.
hints: What's the worst thing that can happen to a user file? That tells you the headline NFR.
Sync latency is user-visible. Pin a number — seconds, not minutes — and quantify total storage at scale.
Bandwidth efficiency matters when files are large and changes are small. What does that imply for your upload protocol later?

stages.title: Core Entities
stages.howToAnswer: Nouns only. Don't define schemas yet.

avoid: Adding entities the requirements don't justify

stages.sampleAnswer:
- User: who owns the files.
- File: a logical file (path, name, current version).
- FileBlock: a chunk of a file's content, content-addressed.
- Device: an installation that syncs.
hints: Distinguish a logical File from the bytes it's made of — they have different lifecycles and different access patterns.
Add a Device only if your sync model needs to address one specifically. List share-related entities only if sharing is in scope.

stages.title: API
stages.howToAnswer: Upload, download, list/sync changes, share. Show what's in the body and what comes back.

must: Sync / list-changes endpoint that returns deltas since a cursor
should: Long-polling or websocket for sync notifications
avoid: Sending entire file content over a single REST POST for large files
Pull-only sync with no push channel

hints: Three categories: upload, download, and 'has anything changed since I last looked?'.
Sending an entire 5GB file as one POST is a non-starter — what's the right granularity? How does the client know what to send?
Sync needs both a poll mode and a push mode. Why both? Think about reconnection and missed events.

stages.title: High-Level Design
stages.questionPrompt: Sketch the architecture and walk through the upload/sync paths.
stages.howToAnswer: Show: client → API → metadata DB + blob store. Add a notification path for sync. Mention dedupe by block hash.

must: Separation of metadata DB and blob storage
Push channel for sync (websocket or long poll)
avoid: Storing file bytes in the metadata database

stages.sampleAnswer:
Client computes SHA-256 of each 4MB block before uploading. Calls POST /files/upload with the block hashes. Server checks which hashes are missing in the blob store; client uploads only those via PUT /blocks/:hash to S3-compatible storage.

Metadata (file paths, current block list per file, version, owner) lives in a sharded relational store keyed by user_id.

On write, server appends an entry to a per-user change log and publishes a notification on a Pub/Sub topic the user's devices subscribe to via websocket. Devices then call GET /sync?cursor=... to pull the deltas.

Downloads go via CDN edge → blob store.
hints: Two stores: one for metadata (paths, ownership, version), one for bytes. What goes where, and why never mix them?
Block-level dedupe is the whole game. What's the unit, and how does the server know which blocks the client already has?
Sync needs a notification path. What does the server publish on a write, and how does the client turn that into 'pull these deltas'?

deepDives.title: Large file uploads
deepDives.questionPrompt: How would you handle uploads of very large files (e.g., 10GB) over a flaky connection?
deepDives.sampleAnswer: Split into 4MB blocks, hash each (SHA-256). POST the manifest; server returns the subset of hashes missing in blob store. Client uploads missing blocks in parallel (e.g., 4 concurrent PUTs) with per-block retry on transient failures. On reconnect, re-issue the same manifest call — server returns only what's still missing, so we resume without re-uploading completed blocks. Block dedupe also kicks in across users (the 'shipped iso' phenomenon).

avoid: Single multipart POST that has to restart on failure
Server-side reassembly that blocks the response

hints: Whole-file retry is unacceptable on a flaky link. What's the smallest unit that can fail and retry independently?
If the upload disconnects at 90%, how does the client know what's already on the server? What does it ask?
Parallelism helps throughput but costs memory and connections. What's a reasonable bound, and what dedupe wins do you get for free?

deepDives.title: Conflict resolution
deepDives.questionPrompt: Two devices edit the same file offline and both come online. How does the system resolve the conflict?
deepDives.sampleAnswer: Each file has a version vector or monotonic version. Upload requests include parentVersion. If the file has advanced past parentVersion, server rejects with 409 + the current version. Client then writes the new content as 'filename (Conflict copy from device X).ext' alongside the server's version, and the user sees both. This avoids silent data loss; merging is left to the user / app. For binary files this is the only safe default.

must: Concrete conflict policy (LWW, conflicted copy, merge)
should: Surface the conflict to the user

hints: Without a version on each write, you can't even tell two clients are conflicting. What's the smallest version primitive?
Pick a policy: silent last-writer-wins, surfaced conflict copy, or merge. Which is safe for arbitrary binary content?
Whatever you choose, the user must know something happened. What do they see in their file list?

deepDives.title: Low sync latency
deepDives.questionPrompt: How do you keep peer devices in sync within seconds of an upload?
deepDives.sampleAnswer: Devices maintain a websocket to a Pub/Sub-backed notification gateway, subscribed to topic user:{id}. On write, the metadata service publishes the new cursor. Devices pull deltas via GET /sync?cursor=... — push tells them when, pull gives reliable delivery. On reconnect after disconnect, device just re-issues the pull with its last cursor; nothing is lost. p99 sync latency: ~1s within the same region.

must: Cursor-based delta pull, not full-state push
avoid: Polling every device every N seconds
Pushing whole file contents over the notification channel

hints: Polling can't be fast and cheap at the same time at 500M users. What's the alternative?
Push tells the client when. Pull gives reliable delivery. Why do you usually want both, not one?
What happens when a device is offline for an hour and reconnects? Don't push everything — what state do you keep on the client?
